item.title: How ADHD Stimulant Medications Really Work
item.description:
ADHD

How ADHD Stimulant Medications Really Work

What research on stimulants means for adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Stimulants may improve alertness and motivation more than attention, helping adults engage with daily tasks.
  • Medication works best alongside healthy sleep, executive functioning strategies, and practical supports.
  • Understanding how stimulants work helps adults set realistic expectations and make informed treatment choices.
Source: PeopleImages/ iStock

Recent research shows stimulant attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medications may boost alertness and motivation more than attention. Learn what this means for sleep, learning, and daily life.

For decades, stimulant medications have been described as helping people with ADHD "focus better." That explanation has always felt a bit incomplete for many adults who take medication and notice they feel more awake, motivated, and engaged, yet still struggle with organization, emotional regulation, or follow-through. A recent study from Washington University in St. Louis offers a clearer and more nuanced picture of what may actually be happening in the brain when people take stimulant medications.

Understanding Stimulant Medications

Stimulant medications, including methylphenidate-based medications such as Ritalin and Concerta and amphetamine-based medications such as Adderall and Vyvanse, are among the most commonly prescribed treatments for ADHD.

Traditionally, these medications have been described as increasing the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine at cellular levels in the brain. Dopamine and norepinephrine are involved in pleasure, satisfaction, alertness, and interest; they affect attention, motivation, and many executive functioning skills. Stimulant medication has been proven to help increase attention, curb impulsivity, contribute to emotional control, improve working memory, and reduce hyperactivity. Approximately 70 percent of adults show improvement when prescribed a stimulant.

At the same time, stimulant medications have long been surrounded by questions and misconceptions. Many adults wonder whether taking medication will change their personality, make them feel emotionally "flat," interfere with sleep, or lead to dependence. These concerns deserve thoughtful, individualized conversations with a knowledgeable healthcare provider rather than blanket reassurance or fear-based misinformation. Research shows that appropriately prescribed stimulant medications do not increase the risk of substance use disorders and may actually reduce that risk for many people with ADHD.

A New Way of Looking at How Stimulants Affect the Brain

The Washington University study used brain imaging to examine how stimulant medications affect neural activity during attention-demanding tasks. Instead of focusing only on whether performance improved, researchers looked at which brain networks were activated. What they found was surprising.

Rather than directly enhancing the brain's attention-control networks, stimulant medications appeared to increase activity in systems related to alertness, wakefulness, and reward. In other words, the medications helped participants feel more awake and motivated to engage with tasks, even when they were sleep-deprived. One striking finding was that stimulant medication seemed to mask the cognitive effects of sleep deprivation. Participants performed better on tasks despite being tired, but their underlying attention networks did not show the same improvements. This highlights an important distinction between performance and cognition.

Looking Focused Isn't the Same as Being Regulated

In my clinical work, I often talk with adults about the difference between performance and capacity. Performance is what others can see: showing up to work, finishing a project, paying the bills, responding to emails, or managing household responsibilities. Capacity refers to the underlying cognitive skills that make those tasks possible, including attention regulation, working memory, emotional regulation, planning, and organization.

Source: :Liubomyr Vorona / iStock

Feeling more awake and motivated can make it easier to get started, stay engaged, and follow through. But, as I often say, pills don't teach skills. Medication can improve your ability to engage, but it doesn't automatically build the executive functioning skills needed to stay organized, prioritize tasks, manage time, regulate emotions, or create sustainable routines. Many adults tell me, "The medication helps me get through the workday, but by the evening I'm completely drained." This research helps explain why. Medication may help you perform better during the day, but it cannot eliminate the need for rest, recovery, and systems that support how your brain naturally works.

Don't Let Medication Fool You About Sleep

Sleep challenges are common for adults with ADHD. Poor sleep can significantly affect attention, working memory, emotional regulation, and executive functioning, often making ADHD symptoms feel even more intense. One of the most interesting findings from this research is that stimulant medication may help people feel alert and motivated even when they haven't had enough sleep. While that can improve day-to-day functioning, it can also create the illusion that sleep isn't as important because you're still getting things done.

Unfortunately, medication cannot replace what sleep deprivation takes away. Chronic sleep loss is associated with greater emotional reactivity, reduced cognitive flexibility, poorer working memory, and more difficulty regulating attention and emotions. For adults with ADHD, quality sleep should be viewed as a core part of treatment, not an afterthought.

Five Practical Takeaways

  1. Protect sleep as part of your treatment plan. If medication helps you stay productive during the day, it can be tempting to stay up to "get one more thing done." Consistent sleep supports attention, emotional regulation, memory, and executive functioning in ways medication cannot replace.

  2. Watch for "borrowed energy." Do you power through work or responsibilities only to feel mentally and emotionally exhausted later? That crash may be a sign that your brain has been compensating all day. Recognizing this allows you to respond with self-compassion instead of self-criticism.

  3. Use medication as a tool, not the entire treatment plan. Medication can make it easier to engage, learn, and apply new skills, but it doesn't build those skills on its own. Executive functioning strategies, cognitive behavioral therapy, ADHD coaching, mindfulness, and practical organizational systems help turn improvements into lasting progress.

  4. Rethink what productivity means. Just because you can push through exhaustion doesn't mean you should. Sustainable success comes from balancing focused work with breaks, recovery, movement, and realistic expectations. In today's constantly connected world, every brain—and especially the ADHD brain—needs intentional downtime.

  5. Keep an open dialogue with your healthcare provider. Pay attention to how medication affects your sleep, appetite, mood, focus, and energy. Sharing these observations can help fine-tune your treatment plan so it supports not only productivity but also your overall well-being.

A More Realistic Way to Think About ADHD Medication

ADHD isn't a problem of laziness, lack of willpower, or not trying hard enough. It's a neurodevelopmental condition that affects how the brain regulates attention, motivation, energy, and executive functioning. This research adds another layer to that understanding. Stimulant medications don't simply "turn attention on." Instead, they appear to help the brain become more alert, engaged, and motivated to take action. Understanding this distinction can help adults set more realistic expectations about what medication can and cannot do.

Source: Kanizphoto / iStock

Medication can be a valuable part of a comprehensive ADHD treatment plan, but it works best alongside healthy sleep habits, executive functioning strategies, self-compassion, and practical supports that fit your lifestyle. Lasting progress doesn't come from medication alone. It comes from understanding how your brain works, building sustainable habits, and giving yourself the tools you need to thrive. Rather than striving for perfection, focus on creating a life that works with your ADHD instead of against it.

item.title: When Trying Harder Stops Working
item.description:
Productivity

When Trying Harder Stops Working

Sometimes the strategy we've always used is the one we need to loosen.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Familiar strategies can make it harder to see a better way forward.
  • Persistence becomes less useful when circumstances change but our approach doesn't.
  • Research suggests that stepping away from a problem can sometimes help new solutions emerge.
Where is life trying to lead you?
Source: Gabriel Cirelli / Unsplash

I have spent a surprising amount of my life believing that the answer to almost any problem is to try harder.

If something isn't working, I work at it. I make a plan, read another book, send another email, pin another list, or have another earnest conversation with myself about what I could be doing differently. Occasionally I do all of these things at once, which gives me the satisfying impression that progress must surely be taking place somewhere.

To be fair, this strategy has served me rather well.

I have written books, built businesses, moved countries and started again more than once. Persistence is a quality I admire, and there are undoubtedly times when the only way through something is to keep putting one foot in front of the other.

Lately, though, I have become curious about what happens when persistence quietly turns into something else. At what point does determination become rigidity? And how do we recognise that moment when we're standing inside it?

The Einstellung Effect

Psychologists have been interested in this question for a long time. In the 1940s, psychologist Abraham Luchins demonstrated something that became known as the Einstellung effect. "Einstellung" roughly translates from German as "attitude" or "setting," and the idea is wonderfully simple. Once we have learned a successful way of solving a problem, we tend to keep using it, even when a simpler or better solution is staring us in the face.

It makes sense. Our brains are efficient creatures. If something worked yesterday, why waste precious energy reinventing it today? The difficulty comes when yesterday's solution meets today's problem.

I see this everywhere now that I am looking for it. The person who has built a successful career through sheer hard work responds to exhaustion by working harder. The anxious person tries to think their way to certainty. The perfectionist responds to disappointment by raising the bar. The person lying awake at three in the morning becomes increasingly determined to fall asleep. I've done versions of all of these.

What fascinates me is that the strategies themselves are rarely foolish. Usually, they developed for a very good reason. Perhaps being organised once created safety in a chaotic environment. Achievement brought praise or belonging. Thinking things through helped us avoid mistakes. Working hard opened doors.

Eventually these strategies become so familiar that they disappear from view. We stop experiencing them as strategies and begin experiencing them as personality.

"I'm just someone who likes to be organised."

"I've always been a hard worker."

"I need to understand things."

And then life changes.

The old key no longer fits the new lock, so naturally we try turning it harder.

Cognitive Flexibility

Research into cognitive flexibility explores our ability to adjust our thinking and behaviour as circumstances change. It is an essential part of learning, problem-solving, and adapting to new environments.

Perhaps the interesting part, at least for everyday life, is how difficult it can be to notice that the conditions have changed at all.

When effort has been rewarded throughout our lives, easing off can feel irresponsible. When control has helped us feel safe, surrender can feel dangerous. When thinking has solved countless problems, stepping away from a problem can feel suspiciously like giving up.

Yet most of us have experienced the strange intelligence that sometimes appears when we do exactly that.

The answer that arrives on a walk after hours spent staring at a screen. The name we remember the moment we stop trying to remember it. The problem that looks different after a night's sleep. Or the conversation we suddenly know how to have once we have stopped rehearsing it.

Creativity researchers sometimes call this incubation: the curious phenomenon whereby stepping away from a problem can improve our chances of solving it later. A meta-analysis of studies on incubation found an overall benefit to putting a problem aside for a while, although how much it helps depends on the kind of problem and what we do during the break.

The mind, it seems, does not necessarily stop working simply because we have stopped consciously working on it. I find this enormously reassuring, and it makes me wonder how many areas of life might benefit from a little less interference.

Meditation has taught me something similar over the years. So has writing. There comes a point in both when effort becomes counterproductive. If I chase the perfect sentence, it usually runs faster. If I sit quietly enough, occasionally it wanders back of its own accord.

Perhaps this is also why we can experience such relief when we finally cry, laugh, sleep, walk, dance, pray, stare at the sea, or do something gloriously unproductive. For a while, the part of us that has been gripping the problem loosens its fingers.

The problem may still be there when we return, of course. Life rarely rearranges itself simply because we've taken a walk. But sometimes we have rearranged ourselves. And from there, something we couldn't see before becomes visible.

I am still a great believer in persistence. There are things in my life that exist only because I refused to give up on them. Yet I'm beginning to understand that perseverance requires more flexibility than I once thought. Sometimes persistence means continuing to pursue what matters while allowing our method of getting there to change.

Perhaps that's one of the harder lessons of growing older. We accumulate an impressive collection of strategies for navigating life, and then life occasionally has the audacity to change the rules. When that happens, trying harder can feel like the safest response because it is the one we know best.

I am learning to ask a different question.

When something isn't working, before I make another plan or add another item to the list, I try to wonder whether the problem really needs more effort from me.

Perhaps getting unstuck sometimes begins by loosening our grip long enough to notice where life is trying to lead us next.

item.title: What Keeps You From Feeling Truly Loved
item.description:
Identity

What Keeps You From Feeling Truly Loved

When performance causes an inner division.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us build protective identities and then mistake them for who we are.
  • The gap between our inner life and outer performance often costs us our equilibrium.
  • True belonging depends on being known, not merely accepted.
The true cost of performance
Source: LucidSurf / iStock

Some of the heaviest burdens my patients have carried have never appeared on an MRI, a blood test, or a medical record.

They arrive smiling. They apologise for taking up my time. They reassure me that they are coping, that things are “not too bad,” or that others have far greater problems than their own. Outwardly, many appear remarkably capable. They have built successful careers, raised families, cared for ageing parents, and carried significant responsibility with grace.

The Gap Between Outer Success and Inner Suffering

Yet, over the years, I have become increasingly curious about a different kind of suffering—one that rarely appears in a medical history. I wonder whether some of our exhaustion arises from the effort of becoming the person we believe the world needs us to be.

We speak a great deal about stress, burnout, and mental health, and rightly so. Yet beneath these experiences there can be something more subtle: a widening gap between our inner lives and the face we present to the world. It may exist unnoticed for years, until we realise that we have become highly accomplished at fulfilling our responsibilities while feeling strangely disconnected from ourselves.

None of us begins life this way. Children laugh wholeheartedly, cry without embarrassment, and express delight, anger, and disappointment with remarkable honesty.

Gradually, life teaches us lessons. We learn kindness, consideration, and self-control. But we may also absorb the belief that love and acceptance are conditional. We notice that achievement is praised, that being helpful earns approval, that remaining cheerful keeps the peace, or that expressing sadness, fear, or anger makes other people uncomfortable. Slowly, we adapt.

Perhaps we become the dependable one, the peacemaker or the achiever who derives a sense of worth from being indispensable. Perhaps we become the person who never asks for help because we have quietly concluded that needing others is a sign of weakness.

The psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott described something similar in what he called the False Self, a self assembled to secure safety and approval rather than express what is genuinely felt. These identities are not signs of dishonesty. They are often remarkably intelligent responses to the environments in which we grow up, helping us preserve important relationships and navigate experiences that might otherwise overwhelm us.

The difficulty arises when we forget that they were adaptations at all. What once protected us gradually becomes the person we believe ourselves to be. The role begins to feel less like a choice and more like an obligation, until we scarcely notice how rarely we ask ourselves a simpler question: What am I actually feeling?

I encounter this surprisingly often in medicine. It may be the senior executive so identified with competence that asking for help feels impossible, the parent who has concluded that everyone else’s needs matter more than their own, or the healthcare professional who can sit compassionately with another person’s suffering yet struggles to acknowledge their own.

Beneath these different lives can lie the same conviction: that love, acceptance, or belonging depend upon continuing to be the person everyone else relies upon.

The body, however, may tell a different story.

Neuroscientist Bruce McEwen described the cumulative burden of chronic stress and adaptation as allostatic load—the wear and tear placed upon the body over time.

Most people would never describe their experience in those terms. They tell me instead that they are exhausted, although they cannot explain why. They sleep but never seem refreshed. Their patience is shorter, relationships require more effort, and they feel strangely detached from a life that, from the outside, appears to be going well.

They are tired from carrying an identity that no longer fits.

There is another consequence that may be even more significant. When the version of ourselves receiving affection, admiration, or approval has been carefully edited, a quiet uncertainty remains. We may be loved and appreciated, yet still wonder whether anyone truly knows us. If our relationships depend upon maintaining the performance, how can they reassure the person hidden behind it?

The masks we wear to earn love can become the very barriers that prevent us from receiving it.

Brené Brown’s research on shame and vulnerability points to something similar: Our fear of being truly seen can keep us from real connection. The strategies we adopt to belong can, over time, leave us feeling profoundly alone.

How Performance Creates Loneliness Even in Company

This may help explain why loneliness is not always the absence of company. People can be surrounded by family, friends, and colleagues who care deeply for them yet still experience an aching sense of isolation. What is missing is the experience of being known without needing to perform.

One of the privileges of medicine is that patients often tell us the truth just as they are leaving the room. A hand is already on the door handle when someone turns back and says, almost as an afterthought, “Actually, there is something I haven’t told you.”

There is often a long, strangely gentle silence after those words. It is as though the effort of holding everything together has briefly been suspended. I have rarely experienced these moments as signs of weakness. More often, they feel like the beginning of trust.

Perhaps this is where medicine and love meet.

When we speak of healing, we naturally think of reducing symptoms, restoring function, and preventing disease. Yet healing has another dimension that is harder to measure. It is the gradual restoration of coherence—the experience of no longer feeling divided between our inner lives and the person we present to the world.

When we no longer invest so much energy in protecting an identity that has outlived its purpose, something within us begins to settle. We become more present, more compassionate toward ourselves and, perhaps surprisingly, more available to others.

The Desire to Be Known for Who We Are

There comes a point in every life when survival is no longer enough. Quietly, another longing begins to emerge. We find ourselves wanting not simply to function but to live more wholeheartedly; not simply to be admired for the role we perform but to be known for who we are.

Perhaps this, too, is part of what healing looks like. Not that we finally become worthy of love, but that we gradually realise we never needed to pretend in order to receive it.

item.title: What a 20-Minute ADHD Evaluation Can and Can't Tell You
item.description:
ADHD

What a 20-Minute ADHD Evaluation Can and Can't Tell You

Telehealth solved a real access problem. The ADHD diagnosis still takes an hour.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Direct-to-consumer ADHD platforms removed real barriers, and many adults got correct diagnoses through them.
  • A DSM-5-TR ADHD diagnosis requires childhood history, impairment in two settings, and ruling out mimics.
  • Evaluation depth matters far more than whether the visit happens by video or in an office.

Direct-to-consumer attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) telehealth platforms typically deliver a 20-to-30-minute video visit supported by a self-report rating scale. Wait times for a traditional psychiatric evaluation in much of the country run months. Those two facts explain almost everything about why these platforms grew so fast, and both belong in any honest discussion of them.

I want to start with what the platforms got right, because the criticism is usually one-sided. They solved an access problem that was real and, in parts of the country, severe. They removed geography, scheduling friction, and a great deal of stigma. A large number of adults, particularly women whose ADHD had been missed for decades, received a correct diagnosis and effective treatment they wouldn't otherwise have pursued. That's a genuine public health contribution, and I treat patients by telehealth myself across four states, so none of what follows is an argument against the screen.

The limitation lives in evaluation depth. A video connection can carry a full evaluation. A 20-minute slot cannot.

What the Diagnosis Actually Requires

A useful comparison comes from ordinary primary care. One elevated blood pressure reading in a doctor's office earns you a follow-up. It doesn't earn you a diagnosis of hypertension or a prescription, because plenty of things produce one high reading. A positive score on an ADHD rating scale works the same way. Instruments like the ASRS have high sensitivity and modest specificity, which is technical language for: They're built to catch nearly everyone who might have ADHD, at the cost of also flagging many people who don't. They identify who should be evaluated. They were never designed to complete the evaluation, and using the screen as the decision inverts their purpose.

What the actual diagnostic criteria require takes time to establish. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) asks for three things a brief visit rarely covers.

  1. Symptoms before age 12: ADHD is a developmental condition. Establishing childhood onset takes real history-taking: school patterns, report card themes, what parents and teachers kept saying year after year. This is the criterion most often skipped in brief evaluations, and skipping it produces errors in both directions.
  2. Impairment in two or more settings: Difficulty concentrating only at work, with a smooth home life and intact friendships, points somewhere other than ADHD.
  3. Ruling out the mimics: This is the longest part of a proper evaluation, because the list of conditions that produce a positive ADHD screen is long: obstructive sleep apnea and chronic short sleep, thyroid dysfunction, anxiety disorders, depression, trauma, daily cannabis use, autism, bipolar disorder. Each of these can generate genuine, measurable concentration problems. Prescribing a stimulant to someone whose underlying problem is untreated sleep apnea or an anxiety disorder tends to make that problem worse. Prescribing one to someone using cannabis heavily every day treats neither condition.

Notice that the errors run both ways. Brief evaluations hand ADHD diagnoses to people who have something else, and they also miss ADHD in people with atypical presentations, especially adults who've built elaborate compensations. Speed is expensive in both directions.

The Incentive Problem, Stated Plainly

There's a structural issue worth naming without accusing anyone. A platform whose revenue depends on subscription volume, whose clinicians are paid per visit, and whose visits run 20 minutes has no mechanism that rewards the conclusion "This isn't ADHD." Most clinicians working inside these systems are conscientious people who didn't design the system. But systems select for what they reward, and federal enforcement actions in this sector over the past few years have concerned exactly these dynamics.

Five Questions to Ask Before You Book

Whether you're considering a platform, a private practice, or a hospital clinic, the same questions sort real evaluations from screens.

  1. How long is the initial evaluation? Under 45 minutes can't cover the required ground.
  2. Will you take a developmental history going back to childhood? If nobody asks about your school years, the diagnostic criteria aren't being applied.
  3. What do you screen for besides ADHD? A real answer names sleep, thyroid, anxiety, depression, trauma, substance use, and autism.
  4. Will I be prescribed at the first visit? Sometimes that's appropriate. Guaranteed in advance, it's a red flag.
  5. Who handles follow-up? Rotating clinicians make careful medication adjustment difficult and a treatment relationship impossible.

I keep a longer version of this checklist, along with what a full evaluation covers, at ryansultan.com.

The Standard Travels; the Shortcut Doesn't

When I evaluate someone for ADHD by video, the appointment runs the same 60 to 90 minutes it would in my office, with the same developmental history, the same differential, and the same input from people who know the patient well. The technology changes the logistics. It shouldn't change the standard.

That's the practical takeaway for anyone reading this while deciding where to be evaluated. Ask about depth, ask the five questions, and judge the evaluation rather than the medium. A thorough 90-minute telehealth evaluation serves you better than a rushed 20-minute visit in any office. And if you were diagnosed through a brief evaluation and treatment isn't working, a fuller reevaluation is a reasonable next step, since the most common findings are a missed condition producing the symptoms or a medication that was never carefully adjusted.

This post is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.

item.title: What an Earthquake Taught Me About Identity
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

What an Earthquake Taught Me About Identity

Personal Perspective: Restorative justice changed how I think about connection.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Unexpected events often reveal what matters most in our lives.
  • Restorative justice begins with listening before accountability becomes possible.
  • Personal grief can change the way professionals listen to others.
  • The first person we call in a crisis may say something about identity.
Source: pexels-franklin-pena-gutierrez

Shortly after my mother and father died, I traveled to Medellín, Colombia, to facilitate a restorative justice circle. The trip had been planned months earlier, and although I considered cancelling it, I decided to keep my commitment. I am still grieving, and I was not sure I was ready to return to work.

Restorative justice has shaped much of my professional life. It has taught me that people cannot be understood by looking only at the event that brought them into the room. Listening comes before accountability because people speak differently when they know someone is genuinely willing to hear their story.

The participants in Medellín spoke openly about their families, painful experiences, broken relationships, and decisions that had changed their lives. The conversation unfolded naturally, without anyone feeling rushed or interrupted.

The Interrupted Conversation

We had been talking for a while when several phones started vibrating. At first, no one thought much about it. Then someone looked at a message and quietly said there had been an earthquake. The conversation stopped as people reached for their phones to call their families. I called mine too.

While I waited, I looked around the room. One participant walked toward the door to get a better signal. Camilo remained in his chair, trying another number. Across the circle, a woman smiled after someone answered her call, and quietly put her phone away. Those are the moments I remember most clearly.

What I Saw in That Room

A few minutes later, everyone returned to their seats, and Camilo finished the story he had been telling before the interruption. The conversation continued as if it had been paused. As I listened, I paid closer attention to the silences, the expressions on people's faces, and the patience people showed one another. No one hurried the conversation. Everyone had the time they needed to tell their story.

People often ask why I continue believing in restorative justice after so many years. My answer has become simpler. I believe people speak more honestly when they know someone is willing to listen.

That afternoon reminded me that we never meet people at the beginning of their story. By the time they enter a restorative justice circle, they have lived experiences that continue to shape the way they see themselves and others.

When the circle ended, I realized I was no longer thinking about the interruption. I was thinking about the people I had spent the morning listening to.

Thinking About Identity

I am still in Medellín as I write this post, and I keep thinking about those few minutes after the earthquake. The restorative justice circle continued, but the interruption has stayed with me because it connects with questions I have been exploring for many years.

My work on identity restoration theory began with a simple question: What helps people begin seeing themselves differently? Over the years, I have come to believe that lasting change involves more than changing behavior. People also need to believe their lives can move in a different direction (Castell Britton, 2026).

The earthquake led me to think about that question from a different perspective.

Before the phones started ringing, we knew one another through the stories people had chosen to share. A few minutes later, everyone was trying to reach family. For those few moments, nothing else seemed as important.

I have continued thinking about that change because it reminded me that identity is closely tied to our relationships. The first person we try to reach when something unexpected happens says something about who we are.

Research on collective emergencies describes similar reactions. People often contact family and friends first, while also looking after those around them (Drury and colleagues, 2020). I do not know whether I will think differently about this experience a year from now. Today, while I am still in Medellín, it has given me another way of thinking about identity.

The Conversation I Keep Thinking About

Only two days have passed since the earthquake, and I am still in Medellín. The news continues to report the devastation across Colombia, and each update reminds me that many families are now living with unimaginable loss. Like so many others, I keep checking the news, hoping the number of lives lost does not continue to grow.

Even so, my thoughts keep returning to the restorative justice circle.

I cannot remember the exact sentence Camilo was saying when the phones began vibrating. That part of the conversation is gone. What I remember are the people in the room. I remember everyone reaching for a phone. I remember someone walking outside to find a better signal. I remember the relief on one participant's face after hearing a familiar voice.

I have also been thinking about my parents. Their death is still very recent, and I realize now that I did not leave my grief behind when I boarded the plane to Medellín. It was with me throughout the circle, even if I did not recognize it at the time. I listened differently that morning, and I suspect my own loss had something to do with it.

That is one of the reasons I wanted to write this while I am still here. I did not want to wait until the experience became another memory. I am still trying to understand what those few minutes meant, both as a psychologist and as someone who has recently experienced a profound personal loss.

When I think about that morning, I do not begin with the earthquake. I think about the people who were sitting in that room.

item.title: Let Life Come to You, and Carpe Diem (Seize the Day)
item.description:
Assertiveness

Let Life Come to You, and Carpe Diem (Seize the Day)

If a situation seems out of your control, you can either resist or let it come.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Ambiguity is heightened when we feel a measure of loss or discomfort with what life brings.
  • Seizing the day can feel exhilarating and victorious.
  • We only have control over others when they allow it.
Source: Elena Alexandra Vatavu / Unsplash

Most of us want to make life choices that will generate the greatest degree of satisfaction and to decide which will. The first step is to decide what, if anything, is in your control. If you decide that a situation is obviously out of your control, then you have two choices. You can resist the life coming to you, or you can let it come to you. If a set of circumstances is clearly in your control, that is, you can take directed action that will likely yield a desired outcome. Or, you can decide that although you’re able to seize the day, it doesn’t interest you and you don’t exercise your will.

Let Life Come to You

When the situation is way beyond our control, allowing life to come to us is a viable option. The other option is to resist what’s coming. An obvious example would be a vehicle crossing over into your driving lane at 50 mph. You would likely resist life coming to you. Or, you’re on a beach and hear the roar of a tsunami. However, it’s not always obvious whether resisting life or letting it come would be the preferred alternative. Ambiguity is heightened when we feel a measure of loss or discomfort with what life brings.

In 2019, I was diagnosed with Ménière’s condition, which left me immobilized for 2 to 5 hours at a time. My immediate reaction was to resist, which accomplished nothing. By the end of that year, I became less resistant and more curious. What is this condition asking of me? It became only too obvious that I was being asked to get honest about balance in my life. The balance between work and leisure, between alone time and time with friends, time attending to serious considerations, and time living with a light heart. Life came to me with a powerful message, one that was difficult to ignore.

Carpe Diem

Seizing the day can feel exhilarating and victorious. We can feel immensely satisfied as we witness our best efforts yield their intended results. It can be anything from a menial task of fixing a leaky pipe to closing a sizable business deal. The ego thoroughly enjoys its seizing adventures. Combined with willpower being the preferred dynamic in Western culture, it can create distortions regarding what is actually in our control.

Individuals, groups, and organizations are beyond our control. We only have control over others when they allow it, which is also applicable to our own children. Let’s look at some unfortunate consequences that can result from trying to control what’s out of our control or overdoing the seizing.

  • Physical and emotional fatigue. It can be physically and emotionally exhausting when pushing against the tides of life when they surpass our greatest efforts.
  • Self-degradation. It’s easy to turn against ourselves, deciding that our insufficient willpower reflects that we don’t have what it takes.
  • Cynicism. Repeated efforts to change what will not be changed can result in a loss of faith in life.
  • Resentment. The folks we try to control often resent us for the efforts, not feeling accepted for who they are.

It is also the case that we might not seize opportunities when we have control. Here are some ramifications of not stepping up.

  • Deference. There can be the dynamic of deferring seizing the day to others. We can fall into defining ourselves as too small to live life on life’s terms.
  • Missed opportunities. Chances to advance our lives relationally or occupationally are mishandled.
  • Risk avoidance. Avoiding taking risks becomes habitual.
  • Compromised maturation. Maturity greatly depends on learning and growing, and when we stop stepping into opportunities and taking responsibility to steward what is offered, we weaken our development.

The Dance

We can view choosing to seize the day and letting life come to you as a dance. Of course, life will mostly be in the lead, offering opportunities to seize the day. As mentioned earlier, it’s always OK to decide that life’s offering is mostly damaging and sit out the dance. However, my best wisdom is to encourage dancing whenever possible.

Here’s an example of a client of mine, Laura, who found the rhythm of seizing and allowing life to come to her. Laura had been on numerous dating sites and was feeling disillusioned and frustrated. She decided to speak with the young man she was currently dating, exploring seizing and letting life come to her. She decided to tell Brad that she was feeling scared about their relationship (seizing). She remained curious about Brad’s reaction (letting life come to her). Brad told her that he felt nervous also (letting life come to her). After deciding Brad was being honest, she told him that she wanted to continue seeing him (seizing). Brad responded by telling her that he thought that was a great idea (letting life come to her). It’s noteworthy that Laura acted on her desire to disclose her fear, and it is a desire that often activates Carpe diem.

This is a small example of a dance that went quite favorably. However, Laura was willing to seize the day and speak honestly about her fear. The dance often involves risk, since elements of the risk (Brad’s reactions) were out of her control. The beauty of the dance is that it reflects a willingness and the courage to live life on life’s terms. It also calls for feeling scared and having it be OK.
